strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 environments (RoboCasa, GR-1, LIBERO, CALVIN, Franka real-world) with consistent improvements (5-6% simulation, ~10% real-world)
Well-motivated dual-stream architecture that elegantly addresses the trade-off between unified joint diffusion and uni-directional causal approaches, with clear articulation of design rationale
Decoupled noise scheduling properly grounded in theoretical justification (Rojas et al. 2025), with sound mathematical decomposition of joint diffusion loss
Practical efficiency gains (~40Hz with 4 steps, 3-10× faster than baselines) and flexible test-time scaling for accuracy-latency trade-offs
Strong transfer learning results demonstrating effectiveness of action-free video pretraining and joint training on heterogeneous robot-human datasets
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 7a-c) isolating contributions of architecture, decoupled noise, and hyperparameters, plus ablations on embedding choice and MMDiT depth
Extensive reproducibility documentation including implementation details, hyperparameters, real-world setup specifications, honest failure case analysis, and ablation studies in appendix
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (MMDiT from Esser et al. 2024, diffusion forcing from Chen et al. 2025a, decoupled noise from Rojas et al. 2025); asynchronous sampling is intuitive but straightforward

FLARE baseline implementation raises fairness concerns: FLARE was not officially released, authors reimplemented it, and reimplementation uses identical world-modeling target (SigLIP-2) as DUST, making it unclear if improvements reflect architectural differences or implementation choices

Causal learning claims overstated: paper claims decoupled noise learns 'causal relationships,' but Table 12 only shows correlation degradation; no counterfactual experiments or direct causal reasoning tests; distinction between causality and correlation not rigorously established

Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars on main results; success rates reported as point estimates; particularly problematic for real-world experiments with only 7 tasks and 60 demonstrations per task

Non-monotonic and potentially unstable test-time scaling: GR-1 performance degrades from 47.1% at No=32 to 45.0% at No=64 (Table 6); Table 11 shows expected degradation with synchronous scaling rather than strong validation of asynchronous design

Real-world evaluation limitations: only 7 total tasks, 60 demonstrations per task; variable success rates (insertion 29.2%-29.2%, tool-use 56.3%-65.3%); significant sensitivity to visual occlusion (A.11 failure case) not emphasized in main text; single robot platform limits generalization

Embedding choice validation weak: Table 8 shows SigLIP-2, DINOv2, and Flux VAE nearly identical performance (50.1%, 51.6%, 49.1%), suggesting choice is not critical; limited exploration of why semantic embeddings outperform reconstructive latents

Incomplete baseline comparisons: π0/π0-FAST use PaliGemma backbone while DUST/GR00T-N1.5 use Eagle-2 (different backbones); no comparison with UWM or recent VideoPolicy variants; WAMs mentioned as concurrent work but not empirically compared

Hyperparameter λWM selection underspecified: fixed at 1.0 based on ablation on RoboCasa 100-demo setting only; unclear generalization to other datasets; no guidance for practitioners on novel settings

Missing analysis of learned representations: no visualization of predicted future states, no investigation of when world modeling helps vs. hurts, unclear what model learns about object dynamics beyond accuracy metrics

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across simulated environments (RoboCasa, GR-1, LIBERO, CALVIN), real-world robot (Franka Research 3), and transfer learning scenarios with detailed ablation studies
Real-world validation showing 10% improvement over FLARE on diverse tasks (pick-and-place, insertion, tool-use) demonstrates practical value

Solid technical execution with well-motivated architecture combining MMDiT and modality-specific decoders; ablations (Table 7) convincingly show both dual-stream design and decoupled noise training contribute meaningfully
Thorough reproducibility documentation including detailed hyperparameters, batch sizes, GPU requirements, and training configurations in appendix
Demonstrates transfer learning benefits through joint training on heterogeneous data (64.4% vs 58.5%) and pretraining on action-free video (58.5% vs 50.1%), showing practical scalability
weaknesses: Limited novelty—the contribution is primarily engineering that combines existing components (MMDiT from Esser et al. 2024, decoupled noise scheduling inspired by Chen et al. 2025a diffusion forcing, and embedding-based world modeling from prior work). No fundamental new insights about multimodal learning or world modeling

Modest improvements that diminish with data scale: 5-6% on simulated benchmarks, 10% in real-world with moderate absolute success rates (59.9% vs 49.5%), and gains dropping from 18% to 5% as data increases from 100 to 1000 demos on RoboCasa

Critical baseline comparison concern: FLARE (primary baseline throughout) is re-implemented by authors due to unavailable official code, using authors' choice of SigLIP-2 embeddings rather than original Q-Former architecture, potentially biasing comparisons in DUST's favor

Imprecise problem formulation and framing: The 'modality gap' is presented as the core problem, but the solution merely uses different denoising schedules rather than addressing fundamental differences. Claims about learning 'causal relationships' are loose—decoupled noise provides bidirectional dependencies, not formal causality. Embedding choice (SigLIP-2 vs DINOv2, Table 8) shows minimal difference

Significant limitation inadequately addressed: Failure case analysis (A.11) reveals the method fails under visual occlusion—a fundamental vulnerability for a method relying on visual prediction to guide actions. Method degrades to 47.9% success with zero vision denoising, indicating visual prediction is critical for gains; this should be front-and-center, not in appendix

No statistical rigor: Missing error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing despite inherent stochasticity in robotics. Real-world evaluation uses only 60 demos per task and single robot platform (Franka) with 7 tasks

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Unclear which component drives improvements—architecture, decoupled training, embedding target, or combination. Non-monotonic scaling in Table 6 (GR-1 at No=64 worse than No=32) suggests brittleness, with post-hoc explanation about ODE solver gradient errors

Presentation oversells contribution: Figure 1 comparison between Causal and Dual-Stream designs is visually subtle. Terms like 'asynchronous sampling' (just different step sizes) and claims of 'effective transfer learning' (using hand pose retargeting and standard video pretraining) exaggerate novelty. Framing problem as learning causal structure is imprecise given the actual mechanisms

strengths: Well-motivated architecture that elegantly balances modality-specific processing with cross-modal integration, clearly articulating limitations of prior unified and causal approaches
Comprehensive multi-benchmark evaluation (RoboCasa, GR-1, LIBERO, CALVIN, real-world Franka) with consistent improvements of 5-10% over state-of-the-art and validated real-world performance
Thorough ablation studies (Table 7) demonstrating necessity of both MMDiT architecture (~8% contribution) and decoupled noise scheduling (~12% contribution)
Strong transfer learning results showing effective pretraining on action-free video and joint training with heterogeneous robot-human data, increasing practical applicability
Extensive reproducibility details with specified hyperparameters, batch sizes, learning schedules, and implementation specifics across diverse experimental settings
Practical efficiency gains (40Hz with 4 steps, 8Hz with 32 steps) demonstrating 3-10× speedup over baseline VLA models while maintaining closed-loop control feasibility
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for why decoupled noise scheduling specifically enables 'causal relationship' learning; the connection between independent τ_A and τ_o and causality extraction is intuitive but lacks formal analysis, and terminology conflates conditional distributions with true causal interventions

Concerning non-monotonic scaling behavior in Table 6 (GR-1: No=64 drops to 45.0% vs No=32 at 47.1%) attributed to 'gradient approximation errors' but not investigated, undermining robustness claims; Table 11 shows naive symmetric scaling actually degrades performance, suggesting asymmetry assumptions may not generalize

Incremental algorithmic novelty—decoupled noise scheduling adapted from diffusion forcing (Chen et al. 2025a), MMDiT from Esser et al. 2024, asynchronous sampling is standard Euler integration; primary contribution is in combination rather than fundamental innovation

Baseline fairness concerns: FLARE re-implemented by authors (official code unavailable, risking discrepancies), GR-1 training highly sensitive to batch size and required large-scale training; all models use frozen VLM backbone deviating from original training paradigms

Minimal difference across world-modeling targets (Table 8: SigLIP-2 50.1, DINOv2 51.6, VAE 49.1) without statistical significance testing; choice to predict embeddings vs pixels lacks rigorous validation despite pragmatic motivation

Vulnerability to visual occlusion revealed in failure case analysis (A.11) represents a fundamental limitation for deployment in realistic scenarios; no comparison of failure modes with baselines or investigation of mitigation strategies

Limited analysis of what causality is actually learned: no visualization of predicted embeddings, no physical plausibility evaluation, Table 12 shows monotonic degradation but this is consistent with conditional independence without proving causal learning

Real-world evaluation limited to 60 demos per task with only 7 tasks (4 pick-and-place, 1 insertion, 2 tool-use) and predetermined configurations; no systematic investigation of task types where DUST provides largest benefits over baselines

Code and checkpoints not available for independent verification; some implementation details vague (e.g., Fourier-hand action retargeting for EgoDex); reproducibility limited to hyperparameter documentation
